changes.before: Return a callback from makeReader(record) that still calls record.describe() with record as its receiver.
changes.after: Keep a method connected to the object it needs.

before: For an ordinary method call such as card.describe(), the object before the dot is the receiver. Inside that call, this refers to card.
Copying a method into a variable does not preserve its receiver. A plain call has no object before the dot; in strict mode its this is undefined.
A wrapper can also preserve the method call: () => card.read(). Arrow functions do not create their own this; do not replace an ordinary this-dependent object method with an arrow by accident.
The practice callback must read the record when called, not store one description in advance.
after:
In an ordinary method call such as `card.describe()`, the object before the dot is the receiver.

Inside that call, `this` means `card`. That lets the method read the card's properties.

Copying a method into a variable does not keep its connection to the object.

A plain call such as `read()` has no object before the dot. In strict mode, which uses stricter JavaScript rules, `this` is then `undefined` for an ordinary function.

`bind` makes a function with a chosen receiver.
```javascript
const card = { name: "Pine", read() { return this.name; } };
const readLater = card.read.bind(card);
console.log(readLater());
```
Output:
```text
Pine
```
`bind(card)` keeps `this` connected to `card` when `readLater()` runs.

A wrapper function can also keep the connection: `() => card.read()` makes the full method call later.

Arrow functions do not get their own `this`. Keep an ordinary method when it needs the object supplied by its caller.

Complete `makeReader(record)` so it returns a callback that calls the record's `describe` method correctly.

Read the description when the callback runs. Do not save the description early: the record may change before the call.

before.question: const read = card.describe; copies an ordinary method. Why can read() lose access to card’s fields?
choices: A copied function always loses its code
The plain call no longer supplies card as its receiver
before.explanation: An ordinary function’s receiver depends on how it is called. Copying the function alone does not bind card to this.

after.question: Why can a copied method lose access to the card's fields when called as read()?
choices: A copied function always loses its code
The plain call no longer supplies card as its receiver
after.explanation: The plain call no longer supplies card as this. Copying a function does not bind it to the object.

project.title: A method’s receiver
